summary.text: A proton is a stable subatomic particle with a positive electric charge of +1 e.
One or more protons sit in the nucleus of every atom, and their number is the atomic number that defines the element.
A proton is not elementary: it holds three valence quarks, two up and one down, bound together by the strong force.

facts.value: Two up quarks and one down quark

items.prompt: Two atoms have different numbers of protons in their nuclei. What must be true?

options.label: They have the same mass
They have different charges overall
They are atoms of different elements
They hold the same number of neutrons

items.explain: The number of protons is the defining property of an element.

items.prompt: What job do protons do for an atom's electrons?

options.label: They supply the attractive force that binds them
They push the electrons outward
They shield the electrons from each other
They carry the electrons around the nucleus

items.explain: Protons provide the attractive electrostatic force binding the electrons.

items.prompt: A proton's mass is mostly not the quarks' own weight. Where does the rest come from?

options.label: Extra neutrons packed inside the proton
Electrons trapped within the proton
Heavy quarks too small to detect
Binding energy: the quarks' motion and the gluon fields

items.explain: Quark rest masses add up to about 1% of a proton's mass, and the remainder is binding energy.

items.prompt: Rutherford knocked a particle out of the nucleus of one element by collisions, and it matched the lightest nucleus known. What did that suggest?

options.label: The particle was an electron in disguise
The particle might be a building block of heavier nuclei
The nucleus was made only of light atoms
The collision had created a brand new element

items.explain: The lightest nucleus extracted from heavier ones was a candidate to be a building block of them.

items.prompt: Early physicists treated the proton as indivisible. What does the Standard Model now say it is?

options.label: A composite particle containing three valence quarks
An elementary particle with no parts
A pair of electrons bound tightly together
A cloud of gluons with no quarks in it

items.explain: In the Standard Model protons are composite particles with three valence quarks.

items.prompt: At the center of the most common type of hydrogen atom, what sits in the nucleus?

options.label: One proton and one neutron
One proton and one electron
A single proton and nothing else
Two protons bound together

items.explain: The nucleus of the most common hydrogen isotope is a lone proton.

paragraphs.heading: What a proton is
paragraphs.text: A proton is a stable particle that carries a positive electric charge of +1 e, where e is the elementary charge. It is a little lighter than a neutron and about 1836 times heavier than an electron. Protons and neutrons each weigh roughly one dalton, and together they are called nucleons, the particles found in atomic nuclei.

paragraphs.heading: The number that names an element
paragraphs.text: Every atom has at least one proton in its nucleus. The count of protons is what makes an element that element, and it is called the atomic number, written Z. Protons hold the atom's electrons with electrostatic attraction, and the proton count together with the matching number of electrons sets an element's chemistry. In the most common form of hydrogen the nucleus is a single proton, while the heavier hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium add one and two neutrons.

paragraphs.heading: What is inside
paragraphs.text: Protons were once thought to be elementary particles. The Standard Model of particle physics now treats them as composite: each holds three valence quarks, two up quarks with charge +2/3 e each and one down quark with charge −1/3 e. The strong force, carried by gluons, holds these quarks together. A modern view also adds gluons and short-lived pairs of sea quarks to that picture.

paragraphs.heading: Where the mass comes from
paragraphs.text: The quarks' own rest masses make up only about 1% of a proton's mass. The rest is binding energy described by quantum chromodynamics, which covers both how fast the quarks move and the energy stored in the gluon fields that join them. The proton's charge radius is around 0.841 fm, although two kinds of measurement give slightly different values.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the proton
paragraphs.text: The idea of a hydrogen-like building block is old. In 1815 William Prout suggested that all atoms were whole-number combinations of hydrogen atoms, which he called protyles, but better atomic weights later broke that pattern. In 1919 Rutherford sent alpha particles from radium into air and saw flashes on a zinc sulfide screen up to 28 cm away, well past the alpha particles' reach but matching how far hydrogen atoms travel. By 1920 he concluded that these hydrogen nuclei were part of the nitrogen nucleus, a result described as the discovery of protons.

paragraphs.heading: Naming it
paragraphs.text: At a British Association meeting in August 1920, Oliver Lodge asked Rutherford for a new name for the positive hydrogen nucleus, so it would not be confused with the neutral hydrogen atom. Rutherford offered proton, from the Greek word for 'first', and also prouton, after Prout. The meeting accepted proton, which echoed Prout's word protyle, and the word first appeared in scientific writing that same year.

paragraphs.heading: Protons at work
paragraphs.text: Free protons are put to use in accelerators, both for proton therapy and for particle physics experiments. The most powerful of these machines is the Large Hadron Collider. At low enough temperatures and energies, a free proton will bind electrons in any matter it passes through.
